chunks.text: Chen Po-Han is 25 and works as a junior developer at a small app studio in Taipei. His team has four people and one sprint of two weeks.
On Monday, three days before a client demo, the backlog was empty enough to feel calm. Then a message arrived.
The client’s marketing manager wanted “one small export feature” before the demo. Po-Han estimated it at two days.
His stakeholder said it would take one. The team agreed to try.
By Tuesday afternoon the feature had grown: first a date filter, then a choice of file format, then a logo on every page.
This is scope creep: a project that gets larger one reasonable request at a time.
On Wednesday morning the team met for twenty minutes. Their milestone — the demo — could not move.
The new feature was now a blocker for two other deliverables. “We have two options,” the team lead said.
“We can delay the export, or we can ship it without the filters.”
They decided to cut the logo, postpone the filters, and keep the basic export. Po-Han avoided estimating in front of the client again; he wrote the estimate down instead.
The team prioritised the demo, signed off the shorter scope in writing, and shipped on Thursday night.
On Friday the demo went well. The client asked when the filters would arrive, and the answer was a date, not a promise.

In the retrospective that afternoon, the team wrote one sentence on the board: “Small requests are still requests.” The handover note for the next sprint listed the postponed work, with the estimate that had been ignored on Monday.
